sections.html:
San Miguel County is a long, narrow county in northeastern New Mexico that runs from the Great Plains to the Rocky Mountains. Las Vegas is the county seat and the only city. The 2020 census counted 27,201 people across 4,736 square miles. Pecos and part of Mosquero are villages, and smaller communities include Sapello, Rociada, Montezuma, Ilfeld, San Miguel del Vado and Tererro.

Places are small and far apart. A house in Sapello or Rociada is a long way from services in Las Vegas, so a seller there should expect a buyer to ask about access, utilities and the property's boundaries before agreeing to a price.

The Assessor and the Treasurer share a building and work in sequence. The Assessor values property and builds the tax roll, then hands it to the Treasurer in the fall.

Both county offices are open weekdays, 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. The Treasurer also takes online payment through a bill-pay site and by phone at 877-690-3729 using Jurisdiction #4115. If online payment gives you trouble, call 505-425-9377 so the payment is not doubled.

The first half is due November 10 and becomes delinquent on December 11. The second half is due April 10 and becomes delinquent on May 11. Late fees accrue on the 11th of every month on past due balances, even if you make partial payments.

The state auctions property in the third year of delinquency, and the Treasurer can accept payments toward an account only until it lands on the state's list.

The Assessor's yearly calendar runs on its own track: an assessment period from January 1 to February 28, tax rates entered on September 1, the tax roll going to the Treasurer on October 1, and a mass year rollover starting December 1. Notices of Valuation are dated June 1, so read the date printed on your own notice for your deadline.

The state has a San Miguel County sale set for November 19, 2026, at 10:00 a.m. Registration begins at 8 a.m. and closes at 10 a.m. when the auction starts. An advertisement and registration link are on the state Taxation and Revenue Department's auction page.

All property is sold as is, with no refunds, and the minimum bid is based on taxes, penalty, interest and costs. The state issues a tax deed equivalent to a quitclaim deed. A tax sale extinguishes the tax lien only, and no other liens go away.

You can get the sale list from the County Treasurer or Assessor. New Mexico has no right of redemption, but a two-year period under Section 7-38-70 allows a court challenge to the sale. That is a narrow remedy, and it is far better to pay the delinquent balance or sell the house before the sale date.

File a written protest with the Assessor. Section 7-38-24 NMSA 1978 requires the petition by the later of April 1 or thirty days after the notice of valuation is mailed. It must give your name and address, describe the property, and explain why the value is wrong and what the correct one is. The state's protest pamphlet reprints the statute.

The Assessor's page offers a protest petition and pamphlet in English and Spanish. Staff are reappraising across the county, and appraisers carry county identification and wear safety vests, so a visit from one is not unusual.

A county valuation protests board of three decides each protest within 180 days, and a decision can be appealed to district court within thirty days. Residential value growth is also limited to the higher of 103 percent of the prior year or 106.1 percent of two years earlier, except after a change of ownership or new improvements.

Find every unpaid year, confirm the state has not already listed the parcel, and give the title company a payoff figure. Property tax is not prorated by the county, so the title paperwork divides the year between you and the buyer. Ask the Treasurer how a mid-year sale is handled.

  • Call the Treasurer at 505-425-9376 for the balance on each year.
  • Ask whether the parcel appears on the state's current delinquent list.
  • Check the Assessor's records for the owner of record, especially on inherited land passed through a family without a recorded deed.
  • If the sale includes a mobile home, ask the Assessor whether a tax release is needed.

Cash Home Buyers buys San Miguel County houses as is, including houses with back taxes, unclear title paperwork or repairs the owner cannot fund. We make a written cash offer and the owner decides.

faqs.q: Where are the San Miguel County tax offices?
faqs.a: Both the Treasurer and the Assessor are at 500 W. National Ave. in Las Vegas, NM 87701. The Treasurer is in Suite 111 and the Assessor in Suite 105.

faqs.q: When are San Miguel County property taxes due?
faqs.a: The first half is due November 10 and delinquent December 11. The second half is due April 10 and delinquent May 11. Late fees continue to accrue on the 11th of each month on past due balances.

faqs.q: When does San Miguel County property go to tax auction?
faqs.a: The state auctions property in the third year of delinquency. A San Miguel County auction is set for November 19, 2026, at 10:00 a.m.

faqs.q: How do I protest my San Miguel County property value?
faqs.a: File a written petition with the County Assessor by the later of April 1 or thirty days after the notice of valuation is mailed. State why the value is wrong and what you believe is correct.

faqs.q: Can I sell a San Miguel County house that has back taxes?
faqs.a: Yes. The unpaid balance is paid out of the sale proceeds at closing. Selling before the parcel goes to state auction keeps the owner in control of the outcome.
